candidate_relations.reason: Large C2-T1 anterior osteophytes cause the documented extrinsic esophageal compression and dysphagia, but this wording omits DISH and the associated hypoglossal palsy.
Pulmonary nodules and smoking history raise concern, yet the obstructing retropharyngeal contour and dysphagia are directly traced to confluent cervical osteophytes without a lung mass diagnosis.
Cervical osteophytosis captures the bulky anterior bony proliferation but not its DISH etiology, dysphagic effect, or tongue palsy.
EGD shows upper-esophageal compression from outside rather than a mucosal or mural esophageal tumor.
The swallow study demonstrates deep aspiration, but no fever or pulmonary consolidation establishes aspiration pneumonia as the final diagnosis.
This candidate correctly links the C2-T1 osteophytes to impaired swallowing but leaves out the DISH diagnosis and hypoglossal nerve deficit causing tongue atrophy.
The apparent retropharyngeal mass corresponds to multilevel bulky anterior osteophytes, and the neck examination reports normal lymph nodes.
Dysphagia lusoria requires an aberrant great vessel, whereas CT, MRI, and EGD identify cervical bone overgrowth as the compressive source.
Brain MRI shows only chronic ischemic change while structural cervical osteophytes explain the pharyngeal and esophageal mechanics.
Small mediastinal nodes do not account for the focal upper-esophageal indentation by C2-T1 osteophytes or the retropharyngeal bony mass.
No biopsy-proven squamous lesion is described, and flexible laryngoscopy shows mobile vocal cords with obstruction produced by a retropharyngeal mass corresponding to osteophytes.
Imaging does not report a thyroid mass and instead repeatedly demonstrates confluent anterior cervical bone formation.
Bilateral small apical nodules without a dominant sulcus mass cannot explain the direct upper-esophageal compression or tongue paralysis pattern.
Laryngoscopy finds no mucosal hypopharyngeal tumor and confirms a posterior extrinsic obstructing mass.
A chronic afebrile course with sharply demonstrated osteophytes and no fluid collection is inconsistent with retropharyngeal abscess.
No oropharyngeal primary is visualized, while CT and MRI show the mechanical lesion extending from C2 through T1.
Achalasia would not produce the focal extrinsic upper-esophageal bulge seen on EGD or the massive anterior cervical osteophytes.
Both vocal cords are mobile and no laryngeal tumor is reported despite direct flexible examination.
Cervical spondylosis is compatible with degenerative bony change but does not specify flowing DISH-type hyperostosis, hypoglossal palsy, or the dysphagic complication.
Cervical osteophyte syndrome summarizes the symptomatic bony compression but lacks the required DISH classification and cranial nerve XII involvement.
